content: 1. The system proposes medication and drug treatment based on specific classifications, with or without qualifiers and additional input data. Health workers are expected to follow these treatment suggestions and administer the appropriate care to the child. The healthcare facility is responsible for reviewing the accuracy, validity, and completeness of the data in the system. This process can be automated and performed digitally. 2. Additional treatments may include simple remedies that complement drug therapy to aid recovery. Health workers should discuss these treatments with caregivers to ensure understanding. They should also provide counseling on feeding the child and advise on when to seek urgent medical attention. 3. The system will recommend follow-up schedules for the child. Health workers must communicate these details to caregivers and explain when immediate medical attention is necessary. 4. The workflows provided are generic and require customization and adaptation when implemented in a digital system for specific contexts. These workflows are approximately 80% complete, with the remaining 20% requiring human-centered design and additional mechanisms to finalize them for implementation. For example, additional workflows or activities may be needed for health workers in specific facilities. Some workflows are excluded due to the high level of contextualization required, such as dispensing (if separate from service provision), facility-specific configurations, and follow-up (which can be automated). Further validation through interviews with target personas or shadowing their work is recommended to refine the workflows for digital systems. 5. Core data elements are outlined to correspond to different points in the workflow within identified business processes. These data elements are relevant for service delivery, decision-support logic, and performance metrics. A more detailed data dictionary, including input options, validation checks, and concept dictionary codes, is available. Data collection should not hinder treatment or clinical care. 6. Some settings may require additional data elements or changes to response options based on contextual differences. Transitioning from paper-based forms to digital systems may necessitate reflection on whether existing data elements should be incorporated into the digital system. Local customization and configuration should align with national guidelines and local contexts. 7. The decision-support logic component of the Digital Adaptation Kit (DAK) provides algorithms and service scheduling in accordance with WHO guidelines. The decision logic deconstructs child health recommendations into inputs and outputs for operationalization in a digital decision-support system. This logic has been reviewed by clinical experts and may require further localization at the country level. Any changes to the decision-support logic should be carefully reviewed by in-country clinical experts to ensure quality care at the point of service. 8. Decision-support tables detail business rules, data inputs, and outputs to support child health processes in humanitarian emergencies. These tables are based on the Decision Model and Notation standard for modeling decision logic. The logic has been directly translated from WHO guidelines and reviewed by experts. However, adaptation may be necessary depending on workflow or data dictionary changes. 9. Indicators and performance metrics are aggregated from core data elements for decision-making, performance evaluation, and reporting at subnational and national levels. These indicators can be automatically aggregated from digital tracking tools to populate health management information systems (HMIS), such as DHIS2. 10. Functional requirements describe the system's capabilities to meet user needs and execute tasks within business processes. Non-functional requirements outline general attributes, such as offline functionality, multilingual settings, and password protection, to ensure usability and overcome technical constraints. These requirements should be tailored to the context and user needs. 11. Health workers or clerks can bypass standard workflows in urgent cases to provide immediate attention to children or infants. This ensures timely care in emergencies.
